title: RFCs & Technical Decision Records
summary: How teams propose, debate and permanently record technical decisions in writing. Learn the RFC lifecycle, the exact fields of an ADR, and who actually owns the final call.

slides.markdown:
Two years from now someone will ask **"why on earth do we use Kafka here instead of SQS?"** If the answer lives only in a Slack thread and three people's memory, the team re-runs the whole debate — usually badly, because the constraints that drove the original call are gone.

An **RFC** (Request for Comments) is how you propose a decision *before* it is made: a written proposal, a bounded comment period, and a named person who resolves it. An **ADR** (Architecture Decision Record) is how you preserve a decision *after* it is made: a short, immutable note saying what you chose, what you rejected, and what it costs you.

They are different artifacts with different lifetimes. This topic covers both, the exact fields each one needs, and the failure mode that kills most RFC processes: a thread nobody owns.

slides.sectionTitle: What an RFC process actually is
slides.subTitle: Proposal, comment window, resolution
slides.markdown:
An RFC is a **design proposal put under a deadline**. Three moving parts, and the third is the one teams forget:

1. **A written proposal** with a specific recommendation, not a menu. If the doc ends "thoughts?", it is a discussion, not an RFC.
2. **An open comment period** with an announced end date. "Comments open until Thursday 5pm" is the whole mechanism — it converts an infinite debate into a bounded one.
3. **A named resolver** who writes the closing decision, including which objections were overruled and why.

A realistic shape at a mid-size company: author circulates on Monday, comment window runs 5 working days, author replies to every thread, resolver posts a **decision note** the following Wednesday, and the RFC moves to `Accepted`.

Rust, Python (PEPs), Kubernetes (KEPs) and most large engineering orgs all run some variant. The variation is in the ceremony; the deadline and the named resolver are constant.

slides.subTitle: Copy this header verbatim
slides.markdown:
The metadata header is what makes an RFC greppable years later. Put it at the top, before any prose:

```markdown
RFC-0042: Move order events from SQS to Kafka

Status:        Open for comment
Author:        priya@ (Payments)
Resolver:      dan@ (Principal, Platform)
Reviewers:     Payments, Platform, SRE
Comment until: 2026-08-14 17:00 IST
Supersedes:    -

## Problem
Order events are consumed by 6 services; 2 need replay after a bad deploy.
SQS cannot replay a consumed message. Last incident cost 4h of manual backfill.

## Goals / Non-goals
Goals: replayable events, per-consumer offsets, <1s p99 delivery.
Non-goals: replacing the request path; migrating the notifications queue.

## Proposal
<the recommendation, stated as a decision>

## Alternatives considered
<each option, and the specific reason it lost>

## Risks and cost
<operational burden, migration plan, rollback>

## Open questions
<numbered, so commenters can reference them>
```

Two fields do disproportionate work. **Resolver** names the person who closes it — without that line the thread has no end. **Comment until** is the deadline that turns opinions into a decision.

slides.subTitle: Silence is not consent
slides.markdown:
A comment window fails in a predictable way: the people who will be paged at 3am never read it, then object after launch.

What actually works:

- **Name required reviewers explicitly**, by team, in the header. "Everyone" reviews nothing.
- **Ask a specific question of each one.** "SRE: is a 6-broker cluster something you're willing to carry?" gets an answer; "please review" gets ignored.
- **Treat silence as unreviewed, not as agreement.** Chase the two teams who haven't commented before you close — an unanswered required reviewer is a blocker, not a default yes.
- **Timebox proportionally.** A one-team library choice needs 2 days; a cross-org data-model change needs 2 weeks. A window longer than that just decays into no window at all.

When a thread is clearly going nowhere in writing, escalate the *format*, not the volume: a 30-minute review meeting with the three disagreeing people, then the author writes the outcome back into the RFC. The doc stays the record; the meeting is just faster bandwidth.

slides.subTitle: Every comment gets a visible fate
slides.markdown:
Written consensus is not "nobody is still typing." It is a state where every raised concern has a recorded outcome. Give each comment thread exactly one of four fates, and say which in your reply:

- **Adopted** — "Good catch, changed the proposal to dual-write for 2 weeks. See §Migration."
- **Deferred** — "Real problem, out of scope; filed PLAT-812 and linked it under Open questions."
- **Overruled, with the reason** — "Understood the cost concern; accepting ~$400/mo extra because the 4h manual backfill happened twice this quarter."
- **Still open** — explicitly listed at the top of the doc so the resolver sees it.

The habit that separates senior authors: **edit the document as the thread evolves.** Reviewer #9 should see the improved proposal, not the original plus forty comments. Append a short `## Changelog` line per revision so earlier commenters know what moved.

Sign-off is explicit and recorded in the doc — a `Sign-off` line with names and dates, not a thumbs-up emoji that nobody can find in six months.

slides.subTitle: The distinction that ends circular threads
slides.markdown:
Most stalled RFCs are a role problem, not a technical one. Separate two things that feel the same and are not:

- **Input rights** — you can raise concerns and must get a written response. Broad: anyone affected.
- **Decision rights** — you close the thread and own the outcome. Narrow: usually one person.

A workable assignment, written into the header:

- **Author / driver** — writes the doc, runs the process, replies to comments.
- **Resolver (approver)** — exactly one person, senior enough that nobody appeals past them. Two approvers is zero approvers.
- **Required reviewers** — teams whose systems or on-call load change. Their unaddressed objection blocks.
- **Informed** — read-only; they get the announcement, not a veto.

Say this out loud at the start: *"Everyone has input, dan@ has the call."* It sounds blunt and it is exactly what makes strong disagreement safe — people argue harder when they know the argument terminates.

The anti-pattern is decision-by-exhaustion: the thread ends when the last person stops replying, so whoever has the most stamina wins.

slides.subTitle: A decision receipt, not a design doc
slides.markdown:
An **Architecture Decision Record** is a one-page, immutable note recording a decision *already made*. Michael Nygard's 2011 format is the de facto standard, and its whole point is that it is small enough that people actually write it.

The defining properties:

- **Short.** One page. If it's five pages it's a design doc, and the ADR should link to it instead.
- **Immutable.** You never edit an accepted ADR's decision. You write a *new* ADR that supersedes it. The old one stays, marked `Superseded by ADR-0031`, because the historical reasoning is the artifact.
- **Numbered and sequential.** `0001`, `0002`, … so "see ADR-0017" is an unambiguous reference in a code comment or a PR.
- **Lives in the repo**, at `docs/adr/0017-use-utc-for-all-stored-timestamps.md`, so it is versioned with the code it constrains.

A useful test: if a new hire asks "why is this like that?", the ADR should answer it in under a minute. That is the entire product requirement.

slides.subTitle: Context, Decision, Status, Consequences
slides.markdown:
Four required fields. Here is a complete, real-shaped one:

```markdown
# ADR-0017: Store all timestamps in UTC, format at the edge

Status: Accepted - 2026-03-04 (supersedes ADR-0009)
Deciders: priya@, dan@

## Context
Billing ran a 2-day incident where invoices for IST customers were dated one
day early. Three services stored local time; two stored UTC. Comparing rows
across services required knowing which service wrote them, which is not in
the schema. Postgres columns were a mix of timestamp and timestamptz.

## Decision
All persisted timestamps are UTC, in timestamptz columns. Conversion to a
user's zone happens only in the API response layer, using the zone on the
user record. No service stores a local-time value.

## Alternatives considered
- Store local time plus an offset column. Rejected: the offset is ambiguous
  across a DST transition, which is exactly when billing breaks.
- Store epoch millis as bigint. Rejected: loses type checking in Postgres and
  makes date_trunc reporting queries awkward.

## Consequences
+ Cross-service comparison becomes a plain column compare.
- Every existing local-time column needs a backfill; ~40M rows in orders.
- Ops dashboards show UTC, so on-call must mentally convert during incidents.
```

**Consequences must include the bad ones.** An ADR with only upsides is marketing, and it is the single most common way this format is written badly. **Context** must state the forces at the time — the incident, the constraint, the deadline — because that is what a future reader cannot reconstruct.

slides.subTitle: Before the decision vs after it
slides.markdown:
They are often confused because both are markdown files about architecture. The tense is the difference: an RFC argues about the future, an ADR reports the past.

| | RFC | ADR |
|---|---|---|
| **Purpose** | propose and debate a decision | record a decision already taken |
| **Tense** | "we should move to Kafka" | "we moved to Kafka" |
| **Length** | 2-10 pages | 1 page |
| **Audience** | reviewers who might change it | future engineers asking why |
| **Lifecycle** | Draft, Open, Accepted/Rejected | Proposed, Accepted, Superseded |
| **Mutable?** | yes, edited during review | no — supersede instead |
| **Trigger** | a change worth debating | any consequential, hard-to-reverse choice |

They compose: a big change gets an RFC, and when it closes you write a short ADR that links to it. Small decisions ("we're standardising on `pytest`") skip straight to an ADR — no debate was needed, but the reasoning still needs a home.

Also note that an ADR is worth writing for a **rejected** direction, if the rejection is likely to be re-proposed. "We are not adopting GraphQL, here's why" saves the same argument three times.

The full path a decision walks, and where it can exit:

- **Draft** — author writing; nobody else's problem yet.
- **Open for comment** — announced, required reviewers named, deadline set. This is the only state where the proposal changes.
- **Decision** — the resolver posts a closing note: accepted, rejected, or accepted-with-changes. Every overruled objection is named here, not silently dropped.
- **Archived record** — the RFC is frozen read-only, and a one-page ADR lands in `docs/adr/` pointing back at it.
- **Superseded** — years later a new ADR replaces it; the old record stays, marked, forever.

The two states people skip are the expensive ones. Skipping the explicit **Decision** leaves a thread that everyone remembers differently. Skipping the **Archived record** means the reasoning dies with the wiki migration, and you re-litigate in eighteen months.

slides.sectionTitle: Why a durable record pays for itself
slides.markdown:
The cost of a decision record is 30 minutes. The things it buys are all invisible until you don't have it:

- **It stops re-litigation.** "Why not GraphQL?" gets answered with a link instead of a 40-message thread, for the fourth time.
- **It lets you *correctly* reverse the decision.** ADR-0017 says you chose UTC because of a DST billing incident. If that constraint disappears, you can revisit deliberately. Without the record, reversing is a coin flip — you don't know which reasons still hold.
- **It onboards without a person.** New hires read `docs/adr/` in an hour and stop asking the same six questions.
- **It separates a decision from its author.** When priya@ leaves, the reasoning stays. Undocumented architecture is a retention risk.

A sharp heuristic for when to write one: **would reversing this take more than a week of engineering?** Database engine, event bus, auth model, deployment topology, public API shape — yes, write it. Which logging library, which lint rule — no, the code is the record.

slides.subTitle: No resolver, no decision
slides.markdown:
The classic failure: an RFC with 87 comments, three revisions, and no outcome. Everyone has stopped reading and the work quietly started anyway, based on whatever the author last believed.

It happens because no line in the document says who closes it. Once that's missing, every disagreement escalates by volume instead of by authority, and the process rewards stamina.

How to unstick one you've inherited:

1. **Post the disagreement, not the debate.** "We're split on two options. Option A: managed Kafka, +$400/mo, ops burden on SRE. Option B: keep SQS, keep the manual backfill runbook. Both are viable." Collapsing 87 comments into two options is most of the work.
2. **Name the resolver publicly and set a date.** "dan@ will pick by Friday."
3. **Convert the rest to open questions** that don't block the call.
4. **Write the decision note** including the losing arguments, so the overruled side sees they were heard.

A decision made on Friday with 80% information usually beats the same decision three weeks later — the extra 20% rarely flips the answer, and the delay is real cost.

slides.subTitle: Writing justification instead of history
slides.markdown:
The second failure mode is quieter. Someone writes the ADR two months after shipping, and it reads like a press release:

> **Context:** We needed a scalable, modern event platform.
> **Decision:** We adopted Kafka.
> **Consequences:** Improved scalability and reliability.

Every field is filled in and the document is worthless. It records no alternative, no constraint, and no cost, so a future reader learns nothing they couldn't guess from the code.

Three checks before you call an ADR done:

- **Does Context name a specific force?** An incident, a number, a deadline, a team boundary. "We needed something scalable" is not a force.
- **Does an alternative appear with the actual reason it lost?** "SQS was rejected because it cannot replay consumed messages, and we needed replay after bad deploys" — a real, checkable reason, not "less suitable."
- **Does Consequences contain something you'd rather not admit?** The 40M-row backfill, the on-call learning UTC, the extra $400/mo. If not, you wrote marketing.

Writing the ADR *late* isn't itself the sin — many teams backfill records for existing systems, and that's valuable. The sin is writing it from what you wish had happened rather than what did.
